The community is (for the most part) good about understanding that everyone has their own playstyle, and to not shit on someone for playing on a lower difficulty. Case in point, I play on standard, not because I cant do violent or brutal, but because that's where I have the most fun, and that's exactly what a game should be first and foremost: fun.

All in all, if you have the 25 bucks to spare, pick it up, and if you don't, just pirate it. In the words of Hakita, the lead dev: "culture shouldn't exist only for those who can afford it."

[h2][b]I originally pirated this game late Q2 of 2024[/b][/h2]
I pirated this game because I found a funny post online saying that the developer more or less supported the act or at least understood the reasoning as to why. And I [u]legitimately[/u] was in no position to afford the game, even on sale.
After about a month or so of hyperfixating on the game I realized that I do in fact want to purchase the game here, on [u]S[/u]team.

From the gameplay, story, mechanics, dialogue, sound design, movement. Everything was very well put together. And that's from the perspective of pirated, unsupported, outdated version of the game. Even with that in mind I genuinely enjoyed Ultrakill.

[h1]Finding out sometime later...[/h1] That Hakita was still [u]actively[/u] developing the game and planning on revamping the [u]entirety[/u] of it, I realized this developer genuinely cares and wants to improve on it.
[b]Not[/b] just "finish the game's levels, get it out of early access."
[b]UPDATED REVIEW[/b]: As of February 24th, 2025, the game received an update which revamped many features and completely overhauled the graphic designs of many, many things. From level graphical design, mechanics being tightened even further for even more intense gameplay, to completely reworked enemies. The highly anticipated "revamp" update brought many new things to the game and a fine refresh and refine of what was already there.
I'm no drinker, but it's "like a fine aged wine." It was already good. But now there's just [b][i]more goodness to be enjoyed.[/i][/b]

Fast forward to the [u]15th of November, 2024[/u], I had moved states and had slowly put together enough money to purchase the game.
Fast forward to a few weeks ago, about the 24th of January, 2025, I actually launched the game and gave it a shot again.
Still a bit rusty, but I still remembered enough.

Ultrakill's mechanics are still incredible.
The movement, the music, the combat, [b][u]you[/u][/b] [u]feel[/u] like an absolute powerhouse with every action.

[h3]Overall this game is perfect for people who enjoy[/h3]
[list]
[*] Loud music
[*] Breakcore
[*] Intense fighting
[*] Excellent movement
[*] Intertwined weapon mechanics
[*] A new spin Dante's Inferno
[*] GoPros with legs
[*] A really well put together story [u](STILL UNDER CONSTRUCTION!)[/u]
[/list]


[h1][u]Dante's Divine Comedy[/u][/h1]

Dante's Divine Comedy was written by Dante Alighieri, is a story that takes place beyond the living realms. Many of you will know it as "[u][b]Dante's Inferno[/b][/u]" as it most famously features Hell and it's wicked layers, such as Lust, and Gluttony.
[b]Here[/b] in Ultrakill, they are present as well. However, it takes place ages beyond when the Divine Comedy was originally written (1321).
Now. Centuries if not a millennia past. Mankind is entirely dead and machines are a supreme force. With nothing other than their wits and a ferocious thirst for blood to fuel them with.
And the denizens are granted a body, and depending on their life, receive a larger or smaller body. This is an oversimplification but I digress.

You play as [u]V[/u]1, one of the humbler machines by scale.
Blood somehow grants machines degree of consciousness.
V1 finds it's way to Hell, but you're not alone. There are others. Machines, denizens, and more. A lot more.
You thirst for blood, as you are fueled by blood like all machines are. One by one, killing every denizen of every layer of Hell.
You are not the only machine who figured that there's nothing left of Earth, to find your way to Hell.

[b][h1]To conclude this review[/h1][/b]
This game gets [u][b]extremely[/b][/u] high re/commendation from me for how well intertwined everything is. Lore is everywhere, everything serves it's purpose. Your starting pistol has purpose. Has lore. History.
Entire rooms serve purpose, not just a stage for combat. Joke areas have purpose. Secrets have purpose. Enemies have purpose beyond combat fodder.

Please, finish reading this and hopefully enjoy the game once it's done downloading.
And most importantly, have a nice day.

ULTRAKILL is one of those magical games that has 0 fat - Every single mechanic and design is made in such a way to compliment each other, or to subvert traditional/contemporary design philosophies. You'll start out with a pistol that can be charged up for a piecing mega shot, but as you build up an arsenal, one weapon/arm at a time, you start to quickly see how much thought is put into every tiny decision. 

      People like to highlight the "Marksman pistol" (the famous coin flip gun), and I'd like to do the same, but lay out how you start to think about things in ULTRAKILL
      At first glace, you might just use the secondary mechanic of the pistol to look cool: flip a coin in the air, shoot it so a bullet bounces off and takes out an enemy around the corner. After awhile, the gears might start turning: you realize that hitting enemies off a coin is consistent, so you start using coins more. Maybe you notice that the coins really help when running away from enemies, since you dont have to turn to shoot the enemies. Given the esoteric spawning of enemies to keep you on your toes (and to keep it fresh), this can really help with surviving since you wont back yourself into a corner.
      Now the keen player might notice something: despite enemy placement and movement being unpredictable, the only thing that isnt, is how you flip your coins into the air. Depending on what direction you're moving in, and how up or down V1(the player) is looking, the coin will follow a consistent trajectory. You keep playing the game and start to develop a rhythm: look a certain way, move a certain way, flip a coin, aim, shoot.
       You start to get really good at the timing, and notice that at the apex of the coin's flight, a sparkle occurs. You adjust your timing to hit the coin right at the apex, and something magical happens: your bullet splits, and creates a satisfying explosion.
        And man, it just keeps going: you want to maximize damage so maybe you swap to a different weapon to shoot the coin. You pick the railgun because of course you would, and you find out that smart placement causes even more chaos and destruction.
      But wait, there's more! 
      Because you're a pro gamer, instead of shooting the coin you punch it, launching it straight into the skull of a nearby enemy, having it bounce off their freshly slapped face back into the air. You see the sparkle again, and you start to salivate: you throw all your coins in the air and perfectly snipe the first coin at its apex with your railgun. 
       The resulting mayham can only be considered one of the most satisfying moments in gaming, as you comfortably obliterate everything in the room with piercing, damage multiplied railgun beams.

       The interweaving of mechanics results in a beautiful murder ballet, and leaves a big smile on your face (especially seeing the majestic ULTRAKILL combat rating pop up; oh did I mention there was a style meter?)

      ULTRAKILL is a triumphant union between classic first person shooters and the character action games that inspire it. It engages the player with clever design, and will be sure to get your blood pumping.

Considering that I have well over 400 hours in this game now, as well as gifted it to many of my friends, I feel its time for me to write my review. I never played any FPS before ULTRAKILL, and it has been such an amazing journey now that I have come this far! The more that you play the game, the more you can tell how much you improve in your movement, timings, critical hits, and all that fun stuff! After Gabriel, I could tell that my skills were getting sharper and more exact. It feels so freaking awesome to pull off crazy stunts, hitting all the hit=stops, and staying stylish on top of that. 

I am however disappointed in the greater community for some of their back-seating nature. Folks should be able to learn all the tech on their own and not feel bad for playing on a lower difficulty than the hardest one available. I say this as a player who gets the most joy out of Standard. Folks really just need to chill out and take it slow sometimes ya know? 

Other than that, I am deeply in love with this game and the amount of friends I have made from it has been so rewarding! I would highly recommend this game to anyone who wishes to have a good time, or even to folks who have never played FPS before!

See, I pirated this game a LOT! And you may think "Why didn't you just keep pirating it?" this game is too good to not support the devs. The gameplay loop is addicting and will leave you constantly wanting more action and blood. Is this game worth it in its current state? 100%. There is enough content here for at least 20 hours of good content, albeit somewhat repetitive. The one complaint I have is that they made the fishing secret level harder to get to! Other than that this game is one of the greatest shooters of all time, up there with DOOM Eternal and Titanfall 2. 

All and all a solid 10/10 game. Definitely worth the $35 AUD.

Absolutely one of the best FPS available right now. My personal favorite. 

Taking influences from legendary games like DMC and Quake is a big deal and I thought that there is absolutely no way that someone can deliver that as a solo dev. 

The game somehow manages to do that very competently. Quake influences are very obvious with a really amazing and skill expressive movement system that lets you build up insane amounts of speed and gives you even more freedom than Quake to zoom around the map, and a really smart take on the ID arsenal that I think gets overlooked when talking about this game. For example the classic way a railgun type weapon is handled in ID games is giving it a smallish cooldown while making it pretty strong. ULTRAKILL amps it to 11 and gives it about 10 (?) seconds of downtime and makes it BLAST. Every weapon is some sort of a variation of an ID arsenal counterpart, but amped to a crazy degree to allow for more skill and creativity expression and prompt actual gameplay choices on how to tackle every situation. 

This kind of leaks into the even harder thing to do when wanting to deliver on DMC x Quake promise. Emulate DMC. I don't see this talked about at all and imo it's a much bigger task than emulating Quake. The whole essence of DMC is being able to be creative once you have mastery of the game and take challenges in a stylish manner. Unlike Doom and Quake which are very much about efficiency, DMC is much more about playing with your food and through a great amount of possibilities finding stylish and cool ways of dealing with an overwhelming amount of enemies. One really good DMC player will play it completely differently than another. It's kind of like playing an instrument because of the sheer depth of the game. 

The dev obviously understood this and has added a bunch of really cool interactions with every single weapon and removed as many of the assumed game design rules as possible in order to give the player a feeling of freedom and power, letting skilled players do stuff like no damage runs by punching the hardest enemy in the game to death and a newbie die 50 times to the final boss of ACT I. It's such a delicate balance to hit and Hakita did it the best I've ever seen outside of DMC. I kind of had to go on a rant because when DMC influences are talked about for ULTRAKILL, most people don't go beyond the style meter, which is a cool addition, but not what makes ULTRAKILL an amazing DMC inspired game. 

To elaborate a bit more with an example - ID games usually assume a cooldown timer which doesn't let you switch weapons until it's 'recovery frames' are over. DMC gives you creative ways to go around that and do combos that are as fast your fingers are by employing different animation cancels. ULTRAKILL does the same, weapons have some sort of internal cooldowns, but you can bypass them if you have good mechanics and switch as soon as you shoot and know properties of each weapon and the variation, which lets you think of your own different combos for every single situation. Mix that with a cuh-ray-zee movement system, insane amount of inter-weapon interactions and the game gives a skilled player enough choice not to look like other players while playing while also encouraging the player constantly to get better. 

As someone who has played Quake for thousands of hours and DMC 3 and 4 for 13 years, all I have to say is - Thank you for an amazing game Hakita!

----The Gameplay----
See that trailer? That's the sort of action you're going to be pulling off when you get used to the flow of the game.

ULTRAKILL is made by a developer who knows his audience, and his gameplay design choices show it. In this early access build, you have an arsenal of five different guns with two or more alternate versions which you can carry all at once, and two different fists. They all have their unique uses. My favorite guns are the Marksman Revolver (which allows you to pull off a skillshot by hitting an airborne coin) and the Pump Charge Shotgun (which allows you to charge up the power of your shotgun and makes you explode if you overcharge, wiping out enemies around you). The variety of this game lends to the player being encouraged to swap weapons frequently to avoid the animations and fire guns faster.

The game is also described by New Blood as "Devil May Quake". The Quake influences are in the look of the game and the Devil May Cry influences are in the gameplay, and the Style Meter. The more stylish things you do, the better your score is and the more points you get which allows you to buy weapon variants. That's not the main draw of it though, the main draw is that you're being told "HEY MAN, YOU'RE DOING ABSOLUTELY FANTASTIC." with every stylish attack you do and the meter steadily climbs from DESTRUCTIVE to SSADISTIC to the final rank, the titular ULTRAKILL. It always feels great whenever you reach the final rank, and the game confirming that you are indeed a stylish badass. I do have an issue with the meter as its extremely easy to get the coveted ULTRAKILL rank by just blowing up a bunch of fodder enemies, but other than that, it really adds to the experience.

The game also boasts a parrying system, where you use your fist to reflect an enemy projectile back towards them which will then explode. This can be used to reflect almost any projectile coming your way, allowing you to build your style and deal a ton of damage to whoever is hit by it. Some enemies can also have their melee attacks parried. It's pretty satisfying to get a parry as the whole game flashes and freezes for a split second, making you feel the impact of a good parry.

The health system is pretty unique. As it says in one of the taglines, "Blood is Fuel", and indeed being showered in the fresh blood of your slain foes is the only way (besides parrying) to heal yourself. The other unique thing is that if you're damaged, you lose a bit of max health, and you'll keep losing it as long as you're damaged, once you stop taking damage the max health slowly recovers back to full.

Of course, as its a stylish shooter, it does have a bunch of techs and quirks to it. There are some unexplained mechanics such as the dash having invulnerability frames, the dash jump which sends you flying forwards but uses more stamina, and that you can jump after a ground stomp to have greater height. There are ways to go even faster than the dash jump and higher than the slam jump, but it does require practice. And as you may have read from other reviews, you can parry your own shotgun bullets. This makes them go faster and explode on impact.

It's definitely a breath of fresh air in the well-trodden genre of first person shooters, and it's easier than it looks like in videos.

----The Look----
The dev has stated that the game was inspired by PSX shooters, and it shows. The textures and models of the environment and enemies are pretty low-rez, there's texture warping, and if you want you can even turn on pixelization filters for MAXIMUM AUTHENTICITY, That is not to say that the game looks bad, far from it. The intro of the game starts you in familiar and generic industrial corridors. As soon as you get into hell proper, however, it opens up into a serene paradise with Greco Roman-esque structures, and every circle from then on gets its own unique look, giving it a major graphical distinction from other shooters.

Your equipment, from your fists to your guns themselves look pretty nice if blocky. The guns themselves from the Revolver to the Railcannon feels satisfying to fire. but some improvements could be made, [strike]such as the drawing animation of the s̶̡̊͊e̵͔̎c̴̗̠̐r̶̳͝ě̶̘̟̈́t̷̹͖͗͠ Revolver.[/strike] the alternate revolver got an alternate animation depending on whether you cocked it after firing before putting it away.

The devs also put in a silhouette mode which turns enemies into colored silhouettes so you can easily discern their presence against the environment.

----The Sound----
Even from the first demo videos, the sounds have always added to the experience. From the whiiirrr of all your wall jumps being used, to the TING of enemies being able to be parried, the sound design is specifically made to make sure that you can understand what is happening around you even with the music going, and for that I commend it. The guns sound powerful when you fire them, even the basic revolver. After hours of gameplay I know what enemies are spawning around me from their alert sounds.

As with the graphics, almost every level has unique music (four levels in the Prelude stages share two songs each), and most of them are an energetic break-core score (made by the developer), which fits the intense action of the game.

----The Story----
Almost non-existent. The most you get is the intro screen telling you your ID, where you are, that you have to find a weapon, and the game re-stating the game's three taglines. After that you're thrown into the tutorial which gives basic movement tips, and then into the game proper. That's all you get.

You can also pick up books to read them for ULTRALORE™, and there are two secret levels that give no rewards but a checkmark on your completion list. However, at the end of every secret level is a bit of ULTRALORE™, which gives you a small snippet of what happened in the world of ULTRAKILL.

What does exist of the story is pretty good in my opinion, like frosting on top of an already solid cake.

----The Conclusion----
If you love perfecting short levels and replaying them to improve your skill, you'll love this game.
If you love being stylish as you dominate your foes, you'll love this game.
If you want to play a bloody fast-paced shooter, you'll love this game.
ULTRAKILL is a fantastic game and I can't wait to see what the future holds for it.

Ultrakill isn’t just a game—it’s a full-blown adrenaline shot straight to your brainstem. This FPS masterpiece is a love letter to the golden age of shooters, taking notes from DOOM, Quake, and Devil May Cry, then cranking every dial up to 11. From the second you hit play, you're not just playing—you’re styling on hordes of hellspawn at 200 mph. The game demands aggression, precision, and creativity, and it rewards you with a combo system that literally screams at you for being cool. Every kill feels like a bass drop, and every level is a playground of destruction.

Let’s talk movement—because no game makes you feel this free. Slide, dash, jump, punch, air-strafe, ground slam—it’s all butter smooth, and every mechanic flows into the next like you’re breakdancing through a warzone. There’s no fall damage, and you don’t ever need to slow down. If you stop moving, you’re doing it wrong. Ultrakill teaches you how to play fast and aggressive, but it never holds your hand. The devs trust you, and that trust feels empowering.

The combat. It’s surgical chaos. You’ve got a full arsenal of weapons, each with alt-fires and unique utility, like coin-shooting trickshots or railgun nukes. And you’re not just shooting—you’re feeding. You restore health by bathing in your enemies’ blood. It’s disgustingly metal and wildly satisfying. The game makes you feel like a death god with a flair for theatrics. Every encounter is a chance to get flashy, experiment, and go absolutely feral.

What really elevates Ultrakill is its style system. Think Devil May Cry, but for an FPS. You’re graded on how varied, fast, and creative your kills are. It’s not just about surviving—it’s about thriving. You’ll find yourself juggling enemies midair, bouncing coins off walls for trickshots, and mixing up melee and gunplay just to see if you can. Getting that S rank? It hits different. It’s a rush of validation that keeps you chasing mastery like a demon-hunting junkie.

And yo, the level design? Straight-up art. Every stage introduces new concepts, twists, and enemy variants without slowing down. There's environmental storytelling, secrets tucked into corners, and boss fights that slap harder than a breakdown at a metal concert. The aesthetic is this crunchy, PS1-era retrofuturistic hellscape, but it’s all intentional—stylistic and evocative. Minimalist, yet rich in lore if you’re paying attention.

Speaking of lore, there’s a surprising amount of depth if you dig for it. It’s biblical, philosophical, and brutal all at once. The game’s protagonist, V1, is a machine without a soul—but through bloodshed, it mirrors humanity more than it should. The descent into Hell, the layers, the trials—it’s got a Dante’s Inferno meets Robocop vibe that slaps so hard. The vibes are immaculate, and the game leaves room for theories without spelling everything out.

At the end of the day, Ultrakill isn’t just the best game of all time because it’s fun (though it is stupid fun)—it’s because it respects the player. It gives you all the tools and says, “Go wild.” It doesn’t babysit or lecture. It challenges you to be better, rewards creativity, and lets you feel like an absolute menace. It’s raw, it’s stylish, it’s a fucking symphony of violence—and honestly? It’s perfection in pixels.
